bibliographic_reference: University of Zurich, Ad fontes, Abbreviations
locator: sections Methods and Forms, web lines 456-480
evidence_paraphrase: Distinguishes syllabic shortening, suspension, contraction and special signs; nasal/r marks have contextual expansions; common marks form prefixes and suffixes; business writing uses coin, measure and weight signs.
limitation: Modern synthesis; explicitly warns of regional and scribal variation.

bibliographic_reference: Joanna Grzybowska, The use of abbreviations by superscript letter in an early fifteenth-century manuscript of the Wycliffite Bible, Linguistics Beyond And Within 4 (2018), 51-62, DOI 10.31743/lingbaw.5665
evidence_paraphrase: A period manuscript has context-sensitive truncation/contraction signs; four superscript letters encode seven sequences; one mark is word-final only; the study separates whole-word abbreviations from sequence abbreviations.
short_excerpt: four different superscript letters ... seven different sequences of letters
limitation: One English biblical manuscript, not a technical or cipher corpus.

bibliographic_reference: Universitat de Barcelona, UBTERM, notae iuris
historical_object_date: late-medieval use of an older legal tradition
evidence_paraphrase: Legal technical abbreviations combine simple/syllabic suspension, contraction, Tironian-derived signs and conventional signs; examples distinguish cum, post, beneficio, omnia, per and pro.
limitation: Defines the tradition broadly and does not quantify a late-medieval local inventory.

bibliographic_reference: Isabel De la Cruz-Cabanillas and Irene Diego-Rodríguez, Abbreviations in Medieval Medical Manuscripts, SELIM 23 (2019), 163-183
historical_object_date: medical writing from late 14th through 15th century
evidence_paraphrase: Contraction is common; bars add nasal/final material; brevigraphs encode per/par/pre/pro, r-clusters and s-endings; medical-only signs cover Recipe, ana and multiple weights/measures.
short_excerpt: per, par, pre or pro ... -er/-re, -ir/-ri, and -ur
limitation: Most analyzed witnesses are fifteenth-century and several postdate 1450.

source_level: peer-reviewed study of a dated manuscript
bibliographic_reference: T. W. Allen, Fourteenth-Century Tachygraphy, Journal of Hellenic Studies 11 (1890), 286-293, DOI 10.2307/623435
evidence_paraphrase: A dated medical manuscript switches from ordinary script into shorthand, contains continuous shorthand passages and ends with a formal table of signs and interpretations; listed interpretations include syllables/short words.
short_excerpt: a formal table of tachygraphical and other signs, with their interpretations
limitation: Old but primary-manuscript-based study; accessible extract is insufficient for exact capacity.

bibliographic_reference: Ekaterina Domnina, Nicodemo Tranchedini's Diplomatic Cipher: New Evidence, HistoCrypt 2018, pp. 3-7
historical_object_date: ciphertext attributed to 1440s; parallel deciphering 11 March 1454
evidence_paraphrase: Reports an early mixed nomenclator as 81 signs divided into 36 letters, 4 doubles, 1 null, 30 syllables and 11 words; later key has 253 signs divided 55/12/8/65/113; values evolved.
short_excerpt: 81 signs: 36 for letters, 4 for double letters, 1 for nulls
limitation: The early category counts arithmetically total 82, not the claimed 81; 1454 is just outside the strict window and the inventory is incomplete.

bibliographic_reference: Barbara Obrist, Visualization in Medieval Alchemy, HYLE 9.2 (2003), 131-170
evidence_paraphrase: Greek alchemy used symbolic signs, but in the Latin West they remained sporadic; early-fifteenth-century examples mix planetary, magical, dot/circle and alphabetic signs; local vocabularies and secrecy prevailed.
short_excerpt: remained sporadic in the Latin West
limitation: Survey addresses visualization broadly, not a statistical sign inventory.

bibliographic_reference: Science History Institute, Alchemical Miscellany, MS 2
evidence_paraphrase: A heavily used Latin/Italian practical and theoretical alchemical miscellany contains recipes for mercury/alcohol and instrument drawings, confirming mixed prose, recipe and image practice near the boundary date.
limitation: Likely starts at or after 1450; it does not itself establish a compositional sign grammar.

bibliographic_reference: Anna Maria Busse Berger, Notation mensuraliste et autres systèmes de mesure au XIVe siècle, Médiévales 32 (1997), 31-45, DOI 10.3406/medi.1997.1379
evidence_paraphrase: Five duration values are decomposed in two or three parts under signs placed at the beginning of pieces; rhythmic value is a function of symbol and mensural context.
short_excerpt: décomposée chacune des cinq différentes durées de notes
limitation: Nonlinguistic output makes this a formal-control system only.

bibliographic_reference: University of Basel, Ligatures as rhythmic figures
historical_object_date: developed after 1250 and continued into later medieval notation
evidence_paraphrase: Ligature shape, initial stem, relative position and neighboring context jointly determine sequences of long, breve and semibreve values.
short_excerpt: read in the context of the neighbouring notes
limitation: Core examples are thirteenth-century antecedents, not a 1350-1450 linguistic code.

source_level: dissertation based on primary account books
bibliographic_reference: Franz-Josef Arlinghaus, Zwischen Notiz und Bilanz: Datini/di Berto-Handlungsgesellschaft in Avignon
evidence_paraphrase: The account books used full sentences and complete texts despite knowledge of tabular writing; specialist terminology and cross-book structure developed, but symbol-dense notation did not predominate.
limitation: One company/archive; useful mainly as a negative control.
